questions.question: Is Google Analytics GDPR compliant out of the box?
questions.answer_summary: No — GA4 collects detailed behavioral data via cookies and can be used for cross-device tracking/advertising, which requires explicit user consent under GDPR Art. 6(1)(a) plus ePrivacy consent for the cookies themselves.

questions.question: What do I actually need to add to make GA usable under GDPR?
questions.answer_summary: A valid cookie consent banner, a signed data processing agreement with Google, IP anonymization, a clear privacy policy, and a working opt-out.

questions.question: Is 'GDPR compliant analytics' marketing language actually accurate?
questions.answer_summary: A widely discussed post argues many tools marketed as 'GDPR compliant analytics' may still be violating GDPR in practice — this generated 75 points and 82 comments on Hacker News.

questions.question: What are the main alternatives to Google Analytics for GDPR compliance?
questions.answer_summary: Plausible, Matomo, Fathom, and several smaller self-hosted/lightweight tools (Hector Analytics, Prodlytic, Pulsemetrics, Beam Analytics) are the alternatives founders repeatedly discuss.

questions.question: Can analytics avoid needing a cookie consent banner entirely?
questions.answer_summary: Yes for some tools — Plausible markets itself as GDPR-compliant without requiring a cookie consent banner, a claim that drew 145 points and 137 comments of discussion on Hacker News.

questions.question: Do 'statistics/performance' cookies need consent?
questions.answer_summary: Consent is required for all non-strictly-necessary cookies; statistics cookies may only avoid separate consent if data is aggregated/anonymized and used exclusively by the site owner.

questions.question: How easy does it need to be to withdraw analytics consent?
questions.answer_summary: It must be as easy for a user to withdraw consent as it was to give it.

questions.question: Are self-hosted analytics tools automatically GDPR-friendly?
questions.answer_summary: Not automatically — this is directly debated in a piece titled 'Are self-hosted analytics GDPR friendly?', implying self-hosting alone doesn't guarantee compliance.

questions.question: Does a small script size matter for compliance marketing?
questions.answer_summary: Some vendors market a sub-1KB tracking script as 'GDPR-first,' tying script minimalism to a compliance pitch.

questions.question: Does GDPR really apply to a solo founder's small SaaS, not just big companies?
questions.answer_summary: Yes — founders explicitly ask this in threads like 'Ask HN: GDPR in 2022 – What do I need to know as a solo founder?', showing the compliance question is squarely a small-operator concern, not just an enterprise one.

questions.question: What must be disclosed to users before they consent to cookies?
questions.answer_summary: Accurate, specific information about what each cookie tracks and why, written in plain language, before consent is collected.

questions.question: Should a user who refuses analytics cookies still be able to use the product?
questions.answer_summary: Yes — refusing non-essential cookies should not block access to the core service.

questions.question: Is cookie/analytics compliance a one-time setup or ongoing work?
questions.answer_summary: Ongoing — cookie policies need to stay current as tracking technology and cookies themselves keep evolving.
